papers.title: [Editorial] Gene-editing therapies: delivering safely for patients
papers.summary: “The pain I would feel in my body was like being struck by lightning and hit by a freight train all at once.” Victoria Gray's words will resonate with anyone who has experienced a sickle-cell disease crisis. In 2019, she became the first patient to have sickle-cell disease treated with the pioneering gene-editing therapy now known as Casgevy/exa-cel, which has since been approved for sickle-cell disease and β-thalassaemia. Her medical transformation was remarkable: “Now I can dream again without limitations.” Further successes have followed, including editing T cells as a leukaemia therapy and editing liver cells to treat transthyretin amyloidosis or metabolic conditions.

papers.title: [Comment] Rethinking success after atrial fibrillation ablation: when sham is more than a placebo
papers.summary: Catheter ablation has revolutionised the management of atrial fibrillation. Over the past two decades, randomised trials have established pulmonary vein isolation (PVI) as the most effective treatment for reducing atrial fibrillation recurrence and improving quality of life,1,2 leading to its recommendation as first-line therapy for selected patients in contemporary guidelines.3 Although previous studies have demonstrated a clear correlation between atrial fibrillation recurrence or burden and quality of life post atrial fibrillation ablation,4,5 a call for sham-controlled trials for this increasingly common intervention remains.

papers.title: [Comment] Mitapivat for transfusion-dependent α-thalassaemia and β-thalassaemia
papers.summary: Thalassaemias are the most common monogenic inherited diseases and are characterised by reduced production of globin chains of haemoglobin. The two most common forms are α-thalassaemia and β-thalassaemia, which affect the production of α-globin and β-globin genes, respectively.1,2 Individuals with severe forms of thalassaemia receive lifelong chronic red blood cell transfusions, resulting in iron overload that leads to severe complications such as endocrinopathy, cardiomyopathy, diabetes, auditory abnormalities, osteoporosis, and growth failure, which can substantially affect their quality of life.

papers.title: [Comment] rVSVΔG-ZEBOV-GP vaccine-induced seroreactivity to Bundibugyo virus: a cross-protection dilemma
papers.summary: The virus family Filoviridae includes several species known to cause severe and often fatal disease in humans. Within the genus Orthoebolvirus, the majority of clinical disease cases and associated deaths have been caused by Orthoebolavirus zairense (Ebola virus; EBOV), which was responsible for a massive epidemic in west Africa from 2013 to 2016, resulting in at least 28 000 clinical cases of disease and 11 325 deaths.1 In addition to EBOV, Orthoebolavirus sudanense (Sudan virus), and Orthoebolavirus bundibugyoense (Bundibugyo virus; BDBV) have both caused substantial outbreaks, the latter of which has recently re-emerged in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and as of Aug 27, 2026, has caused 5815 confirmed cases and 2788 deaths.

papers.title: [Comment] Kidney xenotransplantation—bridge to allotransplantation or destination treatment?
papers.summary: The shortage of human kidneys remains a central problem in transplantation, and many candidates die or are removed from the waiting list before an organ becomes available.1 Genetically engineered porcine kidneys have long been proposed to expand the donor pool,2 and over the past 3 years the field has rapidly moved from preclinical models to decedent models to living recipients.3–5 In their Article, Leonardo Riella and colleagues report a porcine kidney xenograft that supported a living human recipient for 271 days—the longest dialysis-free xenograft function described to date—followed by explantation and a subsequent deceased-donor human kidney transplantation.

papers.title: [Comment] Offline: The tragic fallacy of global health reform
papers.summary: In Jorge Luis Borges's fantastical short story, Tlön, Uqbar, Orbis Tertius, written in 1940, he imagines the invention of a new world, Tlön, by a secret society of, among others, astronomers, biologists, and engineers. Over several centuries, they developed “a rigorous and systematic plan” for this planet based not on materialism, but on idealism—the philosophy that nothing is real unless consciously perceived. There are no nouns in Tlön, only verbs and adjectives. There is no science. Nobody reasons.

papers.title: [World Report] Fears over longer term health impacts of Nepal floods
papers.summary: Experts warn of a risk of communicable diseases, malnutrition, and mental health conditions following catastrophic flooding that has killed thousands. Sophie Cousins reports.

papers.title: [World Report] Conflict and inequality complicate Colombia earthquake relief
papers.summary: Health care in Chocó, the epicentre of the earthquake, was already under severe strain. Daniela Díaz Rangel and Amy Booth report.

papers.title: [Perspectives] Tim Baker: bringing systems change to acute health-care provision
papers.summary: “Global health has traditionally focused on health promotion and preventing disease”, says Tim Baker, Associate Professor at Muhimbili University of Health and Allied Sciences in Dar es Salaam, Tanzania. “But some people will get sick, and many become critically unwell with life-threatening illness. Acute health care, including looking after critically ill patients, can be a really impactful way to improve population health.”

papers.title: [Perspectives] A positive difference: unimagined communities, reimagined research
papers.summary: Existing narratives around race and ethnicity in medicine are overwhelmingly negative. Historians have documented overt bias and outright exploitation of Black and Brown people. Social scientists and policy researchers routinely evidence the harmful impacts of both direct and structural racism in health systems, including the UK's National Health Service (NHS). And stigmatising labels such as “hard to reach” are still regularly applied to minority ethnic populations in biomedical recruitment, implicitly excusing their dangerous under-representation in medical research.

papers.title: [Obituary] Maura L Gillison
papers.summary: Medical oncologist and scientist who defined the role of HPV in oropharyngeal cancer. Born on Jan 4, 1965, in London, ON, Canada, she died of small intestine cancer on June 21, 2026, in Willoughby, OH, USA, aged 61 years

papers.title: [Correspondence] Integrating responders’ mental health into the Ebola outbreak response
papers.summary: Ebola outbreaks place extraordinary demands on the people tasked with containing them. The ongoing Bundibugyo virus disease outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, following cross-border transmission to Uganda, is occurring amid armed conflict, population displacement, humanitarian pressures, sustained transmission, and infections and deaths among health-care workers, underscoring that outbreak control depends on a diverse workforce operating under exceptional pressure.1 Responders face infection risk, repeated exposure to severe illness and death, fear of transmitting infection to their families, long working hours, exhaustion, isolation, stigma, and sometimes hostility.

papers.title: [Correspondence] Gold standard vaccine policy as a global health signal
papers.summary: The US Executive Order of Aug 10, 2026, establishing “Gold Standard Childhood Vaccine Recommendations”,1 should be considered not only a domestic policy change but also a potential global health signal. By redefining what childhood vaccines should be routinely recommended, encouraging separation of the combined measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine, and advocating separate medical visits for different childhood immunisations, the policy risks conflating parental choice with the optimisation of evidence-based vaccination delivery.

papers.title: [Correspondence] Global science to promote cooperation and understanding
papers.summary: The idea that science might promote cooperation could sound naive in a world beset by war, sanctions, strategic rivalry, and institutional breakdown. Science cannot stop armies or resolve diplomatic failures. When formal political institutions weaken, science can preserve communication channels, common standards of evidence, and trust across borders. Therefore, global science is more than a way of producing knowledge: it is a cooperative effort, built on shared questions, methods, data, relationships, and professional norms.

papers.title: [Correspondence] Humanitarian lessons from UNRWA's experience in Gaza
papers.summary: The Johns Hopkins Center for Humanitarian Health–Lancet Commission by Paul Spiegel and colleagues1 argues that the current humanitarian system is no longer fit for purpose. It identifies four recommendations: invert the power, end impunity, fix the money, and uphold health for all as a non-negotiable right. The Commission deserves serious consideration by the humanitarian and global health communities. Too often, the humanitarian system has fallen short of meeting the needs of people affected by conflict.

papers.title: [Correspondence] Minority voices in conflict-affected health systems
papers.summary: We read with interest the Commission by Paul Speigel and colleagues1 and commend its timely and ambitious effort to advance health equity and address the structural drivers of poor health outcomes worldwide. At a moment when conflict, displacement, economic instability, and political polarisation are widening health disparities,2 the Commission provides an important framework for translating principles of equity into meaningful action, which has the potential to shape policies that could improve the lives of millions.

papers.title: [Correspondence] Humanitarian crises are a hotbed for organ trafficking
papers.summary: Paul Spiegel and colleagues should be congratulated on their Commission related to health, conflict, and displacement in a world of crises and impunity.1

papers.title: [Correspondence] Naming palliative care in conflict and forced displacement
papers.summary: The Johns Hopkins Center for Humanitarian Health–Lancet Commission by Paul Spiegel and colleagues offers a compelling account of humanitarian system failure and its consequences for people affected by conflict and forced displacement.1 The Commission calls for systems to uphold dignity, continuity, equity, accountability, and health for all. Perhaps most striking is that palliative care remains entirely unnamed in the Commission. A reform agenda that speaks of death, suffering, and abandonment would be strengthened by making explicit how people with serious illness are cared for when conflict obstructs access to physical, psychosocial, and spiritual support.

papers.title: [Correspondence] Inverting power must begin with authorship
papers.summary: The Johns Hopkins Centre for Humanitarian Health–Lancet Commission by Paul Spiegel and colleagues1 makes a claim that is both correct and overdue: the humanitarian system requires structural transformation, not incremental reform, and that transformation is fundamentally about power—who decides and on whose behalf. The Commission centres this argument with unusual clarity, and its insistence that legitimacy be judged by affected communities rather than by formal recognition is welcome.

papers.title: [Correspondence] Inverting power must begin with authorship – Authors’ reply
papers.summary: We thank Qusai Khraisha for a critique that is at once generous and exacting. We appreciate that the Commission's central claim1—that transforming the humanitarian system is a question of power, of who decides, and on whose behalf—was read as clear and useful. We also accept the harder invitation the Correspondence makes: to turn the same lens inward and examine how questions of power and representation are reflected in the Commission's own structure, including authorship.

papers.title: [Articles] Efficacy and safety of mitapivat in adults with transfusion-dependent α-thalassaemia or β-thalassaemia (ENERGIZE-T): a double-blind, randomised, multicentre, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trial
papers.summary: Mitapivat significantly reduced the transfusion burden and was generally well tolerated, showing a favourable benefit–risk profile. These findings support mitapivat as the first oral disease-modifying therapy for adults with transfusion-dependent α-thalassaemia or β-thalassaemia, providing a new treatment option to reduce transfusion burden in this patient population.

papers.title: [Articles] Bundibugyo virus glycoprotein seroreactivity following recombinant vesicular stomatitis virus–Zaire Ebola virus glycoprotein vaccination in outbreak-affected populations of the Democratic Republic of the Congo: a longitudinal cohort study
papers.summary: The differing patterns of BDBV glycoprotein seroreactivity observed between Beni and Mbandaka warrant further investigation into the epidemiological and immunological factors associated with this seroreactivity, including the epidemiological significance of baseline seroreactivity observed before vaccination. To our knowledge, these findings provide the first longitudinal human data describing BDBV glycoprotein seroreactivity following licensed Ebola virus disease vaccination in populations living in regions now affected by the current outbreak of disease caused by BDBV.

papers.title: [Articles] Porcine kidney xenotransplantation as a bridge to allotransplantation: a first-in-human study
papers.summary: This case shows that porcine kidney xenotransplantation can provide prolonged renal support and be discontinued without clinically significant allosensitisation or zoonotic infection. Early cellular rejection resolved with treatment, whereas later graft failure was associated with microvascular injury progressing to thrombotic microangiopathy despite a negative donor-specific crossmatch, supporting the possibility that mechanisms beyond conventional antibody-mediated rejection contributed to late graft injury.

papers.title: [Series] The changing therapeutic landscape of small-cell lung cancer
papers.summary: Small-cell lung cancer (SCLC) is an exceptionally aggressive malignancy: highly proliferative, heterogeneous, and frequently metastatic at diagnosis. Although initially responsive to chemotherapy, such responses are typically transient, and recurrent disease has been largely refractory to standard cytotoxics. The past decade has been notable for major advances in our understanding of SCLC biology, and this preclinical progress is now informing multiple novel therapeutic approaches for this disease.

papers.title: [Clinical Rounds] Oropharyngeal ulcers in Yao syndrome with multisystem involvement
papers.summary: A 41-year-old White man of European and Middle Eastern ancestry with no travel history or unusual exposures was referred in February, 2013 to the Oral Medicine Clinic at Brigham and Women's Hospital (Boston, MA, USA) for the evaluation of mouth ulcers. His notable medical history included depression for which he was currently on fluoxetine and insomnia for which he was on zolpidem. Upon examination, he had a painful and necrotic ulcer with an erythematous halo on the uvula causing dysphagia for the past 4 weeks that subsequently resulted in autoamputation of the uvula approximately 2 years after initial presentation (figure 1).

papers.title: [Editorial] Oral carbapenem—a double-edged sword?
papers.summary: In June 2026, the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved the first oral carbapenem, tebipenem, for the treatment of complicated urinary tract infections (UTIs). While this approval paves the way for more convenient treatment without the need for hospitalisation, it also raises questions around stewardship and rates of carbapenem resistance.

papers.title: [Newsdesk] Research in brief
papers.summary: Although observational studies suggest that the four-component meningococcal serogroup B vaccine (4CMenB) might lower the risk of gonorrhoea, the randomised GoGoVax trial in Australia found that 4CMenB vaccination did not result in fewer Neisseria gonorrhoeae infections compared with placebo. The trial analysis included 587 adult men who have sex with men (MSM) who had a diagnosis of N gonorrhoeae infection or syphilis within the previous 18 months, received two doses of either the vaccine or placebo 3 months apart, and attended at least two follow-up visits.

papers.title: [Obituary] Clarence James Peters
papers.summary: World-renowned virologist died on July 4, 2026, aged 85 years.

papers.title: [Profile] Aalisha Sahukhan—strengthening public health responses
papers.summary: Aalisha Sahukhan was eight when she decided she would become a doctor. “Exactly the age to be making important life decisions”, this proud Fijian tells The Lancet Infectious Diseases, a decision shaped by her beloved grandmother's illness and passing, and wanting to be useful while steering clear of spotlight. Her career, leading the Fiji Centre for Disease Control (Fiji CDC), would ultimately thrust her into the spotlight, first as chair of taskforces leading responses to national epidemics of meningitis (2018) and measles (2019), and ultimately as technical lead and a national spokesperson for Fiji's response to COVID-19.

papers.title: [Clinical Picture] Tularaemia after deer exposure in a vehicular collision
papers.summary: A 39-year-old man sustained facial lacerations from the body of a roe deer (Capreolus capreolus) and shattered glass after the animal, first struck by an oncoming vehicle, broke through his windshield. Animal blood, bodily fluids from eviscerated organs (eg, intestines), and soil contaminated his wounds (figure A). 8 days later, subjective fever, a left periorbital lesion, and ipsilateral cervical swelling developed. On day 12, sonography found cervical lymphadenitis without abscess formation. Despite amoxicillin treatment (1 g three times a day for a week), the swelling progressed (figure B).

papers.title: Metax enables accurate cross-domain taxonomic profiling of metagenomes
papers.summary: Metax is a cross-domain metagenomic profiler that uses genome-wide coverage evidence to improve species-level microbial profiling and distinguish supported taxa from artifacts. Across diverse datasets, Metax enables robust taxonomic profiling, pathogen detection, contamination assessment, and discovery of disease-associated bacterial and viral signatures.

papers.title: Mitochondrial ATP promotes T cell differentiation through chromatin accessibility
papers.summary: Cell-mediated immunity requires cytotoxic CD8+ T cells that adopt and maintain an effector phenotype. Here, D-α-hydroxybutyrate (DAHB) is shown to act as a metabolic adjuvant, driving the conversion of proliferating CD8+ T cells into cytotoxic effector cells by linking mitochondrial ATP production to chromatin remodeling and gene expression.

papers.title: Glycocalyx-edited mesenchymal stem/stromal cell therapy in advanced osteoporosis
papers.summary: Mesenchymal stem/stromal cell (MSC)-based therapy holds promise for reversal of bone loss in osteoporosis. This phase 1 study establishes the safety and feasibility of intravenous administration of glycocalyx-engineered human MSCs and provides evidence that MSCs derived from the bone marrow of older individuals with osteoporosis retain clinically meaningful osteoregenerative capacity.

papers.title: 4D spatiotemporal landscape of mitochondrial phenotypes across cellular states unlocked through representation learning
papers.summary: Agarwal et al. introduce MitoSpace, a self-supervised model trained on 4D lattice light-sheet microscopy data. The model resolves drug-induced mitochondrial phenotypes without labels, predicts membrane potential from morphology and dynamics, generalizes to unseen perturbations and lung organoids, and shows that representation quality improves progressively from 2D to 4D.

papers.title: Architecture of the serotonergic projectome in the mouse brain
papers.summary: Serotonin neurons innervate nearly the entire mammalian brain, yet how their projections are organized has remained unclear. Systematic whole-brain serotonergic axon collateralization mapping reveals five projectomic groups that preferentially target functionally related regions, with each projectomic group connecting to specific spatial transcriptomic and behavioral profiles.

papers.title: Caloric restriction modulates genome-wide somatic mutation in mice
papers.summary: Mutations accumulate in cells with age, while caloric restriction extends lifespan across diverse animals. Grońska-Pęski et al. study the effect of caloric restriction on mutations genome-wide in mice, finding reduced mutation burdens across several tissues and cell types, thereby establishing that diet can alter mutation accumulation genome-wide during aging.

papers.title: Structural basis of a SWI/SNF-associated transcription pre-initiation complex
papers.summary: Cryo-EM and genetic analyses reveal that the SWI/SNF chromatin remodeler is an integral component of the transcription pre-initiation complex. The structures demonstrate how SWI/SNF facilitates transcription initiation through stabilization of PIC organization and concerted remodeling of the +1 nucleosome.

papers.title: Identification of the tendon/ligament stem cell in mice and humans
papers.summary: The tendon/ligament stem cell is identified, and dysregulation of differentiation in this cell is shown as a mechanism contributing to lumbar spinal stenosis.

papers.title: Tabula Sapiens 2.0: A comprehensive transcriptomic atlas of human cell types
papers.summary: An expanded atlas of human cells maps the expression of nearly all human transcription factors across 701 cell-type/tissue combinations and uncovers the heterogeneous nature of senescence across tissues and cell types.

papers.title: Oxygen-responsive bacterial glycosphingolipid links symbiont fitness and immune development in neonatal host
papers.summary: How do maternal gut bacteria seed the rapidly developing neonatal gut? Heo et al. show that Bacteroides fragilis produces a distinct membrane lipid that enables this strict anaerobe to tolerate a microaerobic environment. This finding highlights divergent evolutionary strategies among related species, most of which rely on lipids conferring broader fitness.

papers.title: Ratiometric transcriptional activation by protein degradation
papers.summary: By tethering a protein of interest to anti-CRISPR, protein degradation is transformed into amplified and programmable transcriptional outputs via Cas-based transcription factors, with sensitivity to protein loss tuned by the anti-CRISPR-Cas ratio. These synthetic circuits can be multiplexed to enable high-throughput discovery of protein-degrading and -destabilizing molecules.

papers.title: De novo pan-rhodamine binders for fluorescence microscopy from mammalian cells to extremophiles
papers.summary: We developed an AI-based and principled computational strategy for de novo design of Rhobins, compact pan-rhodamine binders with high brightness, reversible binding, and extreme stability. It enables superior live-/fixed-cell, super-resolution, and single-molecule imaging with properties surpassing existing tags. It also supports extremophile imaging at 75°C, inaccessible with current tools.

papers.title: Cross-species single-cell atlas of the striatum defines cell-type and subregion disease vulnerabilities
papers.summary: Single-nucleus RNA sequencing and spatial validation across human and mouse striatum define principles of neuronal specialization across cell types, subregions, and species. These findings lay the foundation for understanding cell- and subregion-resolved contributions to brain function and disease, including addiction risk, antipsychotic responses, Huntington’s disease vulnerabilities, and pharmacologically relevant species differences.

papers.title: Live-cell transcriptomics with engineered virus-like particles
papers.summary: Najia, Le, Borrajo et al. establish “cellular self-reporting,” a technology to export molecular analytes from cells in virus-like particles. The authors demonstrate how mRNA export enables longitudinal transcriptome-wide profiling of living cells by sampling cell media. This platform transcends the destructive nature of conventional transcriptomic analysis methods and reveals gene expression dynamics in complex biological systems in situ.

papers.title: Endogenous opioid dynamics in the dorsal striatum sculpt neural activity to promote goal-directed action
papers.summary: Cell-type-specific, time-locked release of the opioid neuropeptide dynorphin in the dorsomedial striatum is both necessary and sufficient for goal-directed behavior. Inputs from the basolateral amygdala trigger dynorphin release that engages retrograde Gi-coupled presynaptic inhibition via the kappa opioid receptor, revealing a rapid neuropeptide mechanism for shaping behavior.

papers.title: Predicting cellular responses to perturbation across diverse contexts with State
papers.summary: Modeling perturbation effects across large single-cell populations requires flexibility to capture heterogeneity. By training over sets of cells in a shared embedding space, State outperforms baselines at generalizing effects to new contexts. Cell-Eval, the framework used for this comparison, provides a comprehensive benchmark for future models.

papers.title: Genome-scale perturb-seq in primary human CD4+ T cells maps context-specific regulators of T cell programs and human immune traits
papers.summary: A dynamic atlas of gene regulation was generated by perturbing every expressed gene across 22 million primary human CD4+ T cells under resting conditions and following re-stimulation. The resulting map reveals context-specific regulators of immune programs and links regulatory pathways to naturally occurring T cell states and autoimmune disease risk.

papers.title: Human nuclear ribomes reveal DNA-embedded ribonucleotides as epigenetic modulators of transcription-associated DNA supercoiling
papers.summary: Human nuclear ribomes reveal that DNA-embedded ribonucleotides accumulate at promoter-associated regulatory elements and scale with transcriptional activity. RNase H2 and Top1 process these ribonucleotides to modulate DNA supercoiling, uncovering a previously unrecognized epigenetic mechanism underlying transcription.

papers.title: Virtual Cell Challenge 2026: Benchmarking zero-shot generalization across cellular contexts
papers.summary: The Virtual Cell Challenge returns in 2026 with a more demanding test of biological generalization: zero-shot prediction across multiple independent cellular contexts. Participants will build models to predict gene knockdown responses in a new Arc-generated dataset comprising unseen cell lines. The goal is to determine whether the best models can meaningfully close the gap between preclinical experimental predictions and human biology.

papers.title: Integrative spatial profiling of 3D genome organization and gene expression in tissue
papers.summary: Spatial Hi-C-RNA simultaneously maps genome architecture and gene expression from the same tissue, revealing how spatial genome organization shapes cellular identity, development, and tumor evolution beyond what transcriptomics alone can capture.

papers.title: DDIAS shields single-stranded DNA in mitosis and promotes vertebrate brain development
papers.summary: DDIAS is identified as a factor that protects single-stranded DNA during mitosis to maintain chromosome stability, and inactivating mutations in DDIAS are identified in a human neurodevelopmental disorder.

papers.title: Gut microbiota generate dinitrosyl iron complexes with cardiometabolic benefits
papers.summary: Gut bacteria convert inorganic nitrate and non-heme iron into bioactive dinitrosyl iron complexes (DNICs) that distribute systemically and signal independently of free nitric oxide. These microbe-derived DNICs protect against cardiometabolic disease and fatty liver by restoring compromised metabolic signaling pathways.

papers.title: Synthetic transcription factors designed by domain recombination enhance CAR T cell antitumor function
papers.summary: Recombining domains across an entire protein family, rather than relying on natural sequences shaped by evolution, generates synthetic “DESynR” transcription factors with enhanced function. DESynR AP-1 TFs reprogram CAR T cells into non-natural, therapeutically optimized states and outperform natural AP-1 factors in antitumor immunity.

papers.title: RNA structures regulate norovirus life cycle and enable rational attenuation in vivo
papers.summary: Genome-wide mapping of RNA structure in murine norovirus reveals structural elements whose disruption impairs viral replication in cells and in vivo. Such structural disruptions generate a genetically stable virus that elicits protective immunity in vivo, offering a rational strategy for RNA virus vaccine design.

Mutually beneficial interactions between bacteria and Arabidopsis promote phosphorus nutrition and growth
papers.summary: Over 20% of root-associated bacteria promote Arabidopsis seedling growth under phosphorus (P) deficiency in a host-dependent manner. Further analyses showed that P-deficient plants secrete malate to attract Acinetobacter species to the rhizoplane, where the bacteria utilize plant-secreted nitrogen and carbon sources to fuel P mobilization that benefits both parties.

papers.title: Multimodal brain cell atlas across the adult macaque lifespan
papers.summary: A multimodal single-nucleus atlas of 2,955,873 nuclei spanning eight macaque brain regions across the adult lifespan, including exceptionally old individuals, reveals region-specific and shared patterns of cellular vulnerability during aging. This framework provides a basis for dissecting shared and divergent molecular programs underlying primate brain aging, longevity, and neurodegeneration.

papers.title: Fifteen challenges for generative AI applications to cell biology
papers.summary: Drawing inspiration from Hilbert’s list of 23 mathematical problems that have focused the mathematical community’s attention for more than a century, we propose fifteen grand AI challenges to focus the biomedical community’s attention on critically relevant questions, most of which still lack effective predictive methodologies.

papers.title: Ancient genomes reveal distinct human dispersals and social stratification in the settlement history of western Remote Oceania
papers.summary: The peopling of Remote Oceania involved some of humanity’s greatest expansions into the open ocean. Ancient DNA spanning the last 3,000 years from the Solomon Islands, Vanuatu, Fiji, and Tonga reveals the sources and timing of dispersals following the initial settlement and uncovers social practices of an early Fijian community that experienced recent Papuan-related gene flow.

papers.title: Brain perivascular macrophages regulate endothelial cell function via a cMAF-dependent transcriptional program in mouse and human
papers.summary: This study identifies cMAF as a key transcription factor that orchestrates the molecular crosstalk between brain perivascular macrophages and arteries, thereby sustaining cerebrovascular function in health and disease.

papers.title: Microbial indole-3-acetamide alleviates polycystic ovary syndrome through HIF-2α-ceramide signaling
papers.summary: Chen et al. reveal that C. aerofaciens mitigates PCOS pathology through activation of the adipose HIF-2α-ceramide signaling pathway. papers.title: Hippuric acid metabolism by Corynebacterium glucuronolyticum-like bacteria promotes calcium oxalate crystallization

papers.summary: ILC2s engage in bidirectional neuroimmune crosstalk that shapes diverse physiological functions, yet whether ILC2-mediated serotonergic signaling affects asthma pathophysiology remains unexplored. papers.summary: Hans Christian Andersen’s “The Emperor’s New Clothes” endures because an entire court learned to praise what it could not see. The fable warns that when prestige, novelty, and social pressure line up together, the absence of evidence can be mistaken for evidence of excellence. In the end, it took a child, untouched by those pressures, to say plainly that the emperor was in fact naked. Prostate cancer care is unfortunately highly vulnerable to the same error. Key opinion leaders, professional societies, reimbursement incentives, and market competition all influence clinicians, and new technologies arrive from industry dressed in the language of precision, personalization, and reduced morbidity. Two studies in this issue of JAMA ask that care be judged by its evidence rather than its appearance.

papers.summary: To the Editor Dr Anagnostou and colleagues comprehensively addressed peanut allergy via ingestion, yet one plausible route remains absent from current guidance: parenteral delivery through blood transfusion products. Peanut allergens, like pathogens, reach sensitized individuals through pathways that differ markedly in risk. Airborne and skin-contact exposures carry minimal clinical significance; current evidence explicitly discourages nut bans in schools and on aircraft as ineffective. Although the dominant route remains oral ingestion, as detailed by the authors, the intravenous route has been overlooked.

papers.title: Intracellular Bacterial Persistence in Preventing Surgical Site Infections in Tibial Fractures—Reply

papers.summary: When children become critically ill and need invasive mechanical ventilation, making sure that they get the right amount of nutritional support is crucial, not only for the physiologic needs of delivering appropriate amounts of calories and protein, but also for the needs of the family, where feeding constitutes such an important part of childcare. papers.title: Smallpox Vaccine Elicits CD8+ T Cell Immunity Persisting Over Four Decades with Cross-Recognition of Monkeypox Virus
papers.summary: Monkeypox, caused by MPXV, has become a global public health concern; however, the T-cell immunity against MPXV following smallpox vaccination remains unclear. In this study, we screened the immunogenicity of 21 predicted MPXV epitopes and compared immune responses between young and elderly groups. Two immunogenic CD8 T-cell epitopes, M15 and M17, were identified, both of which effectively stimulated specific immune responses, with significantly stronger responses observed in the young group. Notably, this study provides the first evidence that smallpox vaccination induces CD8 T-cell immunity that cross-recognizes the MPXV epitopes M15 and M17 and remains detectable for more than four decades after vaccination, as demonstrated in vaccinated individuals aged 53-75. These findings provide experimental evidence for understanding the cross-protective mechanisms of the smallpox vaccine and informing monkeypox vaccine development.

papers.title: Factors associated with a willingness to accept latent tuberculosis infection treatment among non-U.S.-born individuals: a situational choice experiment

papers.summary: Pre-existing Orthoflavivirus immunity can shape antibody recall upon infection with a heterologous virus. papers.summary: Wastewater surveillance has become a prominent part of public health efforts to track circulating pathogens and has been incorporated into disease forecasting models. papers.summary: Several vaccines against respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) have been commercialized recently. papers.title: Nine-month all-oral regimen for MDR/RR-TB in Lesotho: safety and effectiveness by HIV
papers.summary: BackgroundIndividuals living with HIV have been under-represented in operational research and trials of all-oral regimens for multidrug- and rifampicin-resistant tuberculosis (MDR/RR-TB) treatment. papers.summary: Sepsis is a leading cause of hospital mortality, yet timely recognition is hampered by nonspecific presentations and label noise in code-based case definitions. papers.summary: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a growing public health threat, where drug-resistant Candida infections are associated with increased hospital costs, lengths of stay, and high mortality rates. papers.title: Strengthening muscle for healthy ageing: innovative treatments for sarcopenia
papers.summary: Nature Reviews Drug Discovery, Published online: 07 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41573-026-01514-3 There are currently no approved therapies for sarcopenia, the age-related loss of skeletal muscle mass and strength. This Review discusses advances in understanding of the cellular, molecular and metabolic mechanisms driving muscle wasting with ageing, while assessing emerging therapeutic approaches and agents in development.

papers.title: Solute carrier membrane transporters: emerging targets in CNS disorders
papers.summary: Nature Reviews Drug Discovery, Published online: 01 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41573-026-01513-4 Solute carrier transporters are critical for maintaining central nervous system homeostasis, and their dysregulation is implicated in neurological diseases. This Review discusses the roles of solute carriers in neurodegenerative diseases, autism spectrum disorders and epilepsy, highlighting therapeutic strategies to modulate their activity, emerging technologies and tools to aid drug development as well as agents currently in clinical trials.

papers.title: Interleukin-33 and its receptor: multifaceted roles and emerging therapeutic potential
papers.summary: Nature Reviews Immunology, Published online: 02 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41577-026-01345-8 This Review summarizes our current understanding of the immunological roles of IL-33 and the IL-33 receptor, also known as ST2. The authors focus on the effects of IL-33 in different disease settings, including infections, cancer, autoimmunity, chronic inflammation and allergy. They further discuss emerging clinical data from studies targeting IL-33 receptor signalling in disease.

papers.title: Epigenetic regulation of B cell tolerance and dysfunction in autoimmune disease
papers.summary: Nature Reviews Immunology, Published online: 27 August 2026; doi:10.1038/s41577-026-01344-9 Epigenetic programmes collectively orchestrate B cell development, activation, germinal centre responses and the maintenance of self-tolerance. This Review examines how layered epigenetic mechanisms govern normal B cell function and enforce self-tolerance, and how their dysregulation breaches successive tolerance checkpoints to drive autoreactive B cell emergence and autoantibody production in systemic autoimmune disease.

papers.title: Immune-mediated excitotoxicity in brain disorders
papers.summary: Nature Reviews Immunology, Published online: 27 August 2026; doi:10.1038/s41577-026-01348-5 Excessive glutamate receptor signalling contributes to central nervous system pathology in different neurological settings, including in epilepsy, Parkinson disease and multiple sclerosis. Here, the authors discuss the need to integrate the immune system along with glutamate-centric mechanisms as a core driver of excitotoxic pathology. They suggest that this concept of ‘immune-mediated excitotoxicity’ can help us develop better therapeutic interventions for various neurological conditions.

papers.title: Beyond the quick win: rebuilding the foundations of cancer immunotherapy
papers.summary: Nature Reviews Immunology, Published online: 25 August 2026; doi:10.1038/s41577-026-01352-9 Checkpoint inhibitors, CAR T cells and bispecific T cell engagers have demonstrated the transformative potential of cancer immunotherapy. However, progress has slowed as efforts have focused on replicating PD-(L)1 blockade successes, highlighting the need for deeper understanding of human cancer immunity.

papers.title: Can immunology still surprise itself?
papers.summary: Nature Reviews Immunology, Published online: 24 August 2026; doi:10.1038/s41577-026-01351-w The discoveries that have transformed immunology often seem obvious in retrospect. Yet none began as an inevitable destination. They began with observations that did not fit, assumptions that somebody challenged, or questions that nobody yet realized were important. Discovery was the outcome. Surprise was the process.

papers.title: Living in the age of inflammation: the reverse hygiene hypothesis
papers.summary: Nature Reviews Immunology, Published online: 19 August 2026; doi:10.1038/s41577-026-01349-4 Inflammation seems to permeate many aspects of our lives, with the incidence of inflammatory diseases on the rise and ageing being blamed on it. Will the next 25 years see better ways to treat or prevent inflammation and allow us to live longer and healthier lives?

papers.title: Building clinical translation on squares of discovery
papers.summary: Nature Reviews Immunology, Published online: 19 August 2026; doi:10.1038/s41577-026-01347-6 Why do so many promising immunotherapies fail to reach their potential? Adrian Hayday argues that transformative clinical advances depend on protecting specialized ‘squares of discovery’ in which deep understanding and unexpected insights emerge, while building stronger pathways to biotechnology, pharmaceutical development and patient care.

papers.title: Why adaptive immunity?
papers.summary: Nature Reviews Immunology, Published online: 18 August 2026; doi:10.1038/s41577-026-01350-x Adaptive immunity is indispensable to vertebrates, yet most living organisms defend themselves perfectly well without it. Here, I ask why somatically diversified antigen recognition evolved and whether its original advantage extended beyond host defence.

papers.title: ND in Micro: neuroinclusion and neuroaffirmation for neurodivergent microbiologists
papers.summary: Nature Reviews Microbiology, Published online: 09 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41579-026-01368-x There is a growing awareness and visibility of neurodivergent people and our needs, but we still face workplace challenges. ND in Micro is a new global network that aims to connect, peer-support and raise the profile of neurodivergent microbiologists and our science through virtual and in-person activities and resources.

papers.title: Prioritizing soil microbiome management and microbial restoration in low-income settings
papers.summary: Nature Reviews Microbiology, Published online: 08 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41579-026-01363-2 Microbiome-based approaches can support climate-smart agriculture by promoting regenerative farming, eco-friendly land restoration and emissions reduction. In low-income settings, which are disproportionately affected by agricultural land degradation, these strategies can improve nutrient efficiency and reduce reliance on chemical inputs.

papers.title: Separating microbial signal from noise
papers.summary: Nature Reviews Microbiology, Published online: 07 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41579-026-01365-0 This Genome Watch explores how contamination and methodological assumptions influence the detection of tumour-associated microorganisms, highlighting the need for prospective, contamination-aware sequencing to distinguish biological signal from technical noise.

papers.title: Colibactin defends honeybees
papers.summary: Nature Reviews Microbiology, Published online: 07 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41579-026-01366-z This study reports that colibactin production can protect honeybees against invading pathogenic bacteria, whereas co-evolved resident symbionts are protected by a resistance gene that allows them to coexist with the colibactin-producing bacteria.

papers.title: Fungal Starship transposons for interspecies gene transfer
papers.summary: Nature Reviews Microbiology, Published online: 01 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41579-026-01361-4 This Genome Watch article highlights how giant fungal Starship transposons may facilitate the horizontal transfer of smaller transposable elements and adaptive genes across species, contributing to rapid genome evolution and phenotypic diversification.

papers.title: The gut microbiota in malnutrition
papers.summary: Nature Reviews Microbiology, Published online: 27 August 2026; doi:10.1038/s41579-026-01359-y In this Review, Littlejohn et al. discuss the gut microbiota as a central contributor to malnutrition, including undernutrition, overnutrition, the double burden, and disease-related malnutrition. They synthesize evidence linking alterations in the gut microbiota to impaired nutrient utilization, inflammation and altered energy balance and discuss microbiota-based diagnostic and therapeutic strategies for improving outcomes across diverse populations and settings.

papers.title: Phage therapy: from basic biology to clinical application

papers.title: Neutrophil elastase-mediated myoepithelial loss is a therapeutic vulnerability in ductal carcinoma in situ progression
papers.summary: Transition from ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) to invasive breast cancer remains a key step in disease progression that is poorly understood. Taifour et al. show that neutrophil elastase disrupts the myoepithelial barrier to promote invasive progression, identifying neutrophil elastase as a potential therapeutic target for high-risk DCIS.

papers.title: Bi-hourly plasma proteomics during the first 48 h of life in an African cohort reveals distinct periods and sex-dependent immune development
papers.summary: Bennike et al. profile plasma proteins and cytokines/chemokines in 679 healthy newborns through mass spectrometry and immunoassays to characterize immune adaptation during the 48 h immediately after birth at bi-hourly resolution. They reveal non-linear trajectories and sex-specific differences especially during day-of-life one, providing a molecular framework for early-life immune development.

papers.title: Targeted insertion of an optimized donor DNA is effective in a humanized mouse model of dominant retinitis pigmentosa
papers.summary: Esposito et al. develop a donor-optimized, mutation-agnostic AAV-HITI strategy for dominant rhodopsin-associated retinitis pigmentosa that simultaneously disrupts the mutant RHO P23H allele and restores rhodopsin expression through targeted integration at the human RHO locus, improving retinal structure, function, and vision in a semi-humanized mouse disease model, up to one year.

papers.title: L013 promotes NRF2 degradation in NRFA-subtype esophageal squamous cell carcinoma
papers.summary: Yu et al. identify L013 as an NRF2-targeting agent that reduces NRF2 via UPS-associated degradation and A51-mediated suppression. L013 inhibits tumor growth in preclinical models, revealing therapeutic potential for NRFA-subtype ESCC.

papers.title: Intoxication and other subjective effects of preanesthetic opioids in surgical patients: A randomized controlled trial
papers.summary: Karlsen et al. show that patients experience marked undesirable effects but minimal desirable effects after preoperative intravenous opioids.

papers.title: Uncovering combination therapies for immune-mediated inflammatory diseases through systems biology analysis on longitudinal patient data
papers.summary: Martínez-Mateu et al. develop a computational framework that uses longitudinal blood transcriptomes from patients with immune-mediated inflammatory diseases to prioritize combination therapies. They identify anti-TNF plus anti-IL-6R as complementary in rheumatoid arthritis, localize the effect to CD14+ monocytes, and validate the combination in mice, nominating candidates for clinical testing.

papers.title: A stem-like chromatin program in small-cell lung cancer is associated with poor outcomes after chemoimmunotherapy
papers.summary: Kumar et al. use ATAC-seq and transcriptomic analyses to define recurrent chromatin programs in small-cell lung cancer. A stem-like program is associated with metabolic adaptation, reduced immune signaling, and inferior outcomes after chemoimmunotherapy, supporting further development of chromatin-informed biomarkers and therapeutic strategies.

papers.title: Dendritic cell centric nanoengineering couples antigen acquisition and STING activation for cancer immunotherapy
papers.summary: Xiang et al. develop a dendritic-cell-directed, dual pH-gated nanomedicine that couples CD47-SIRPα relief at the tumor-dendritic cell interface with intracellular STING activation after uptake. This strategy enhances antigen acquisition and T cell cross-priming, suppresses tumor growth and metastasis, and supports the translation of STING immunotherapy.

papers.title: Emerging role of GLP-1 mono, dual, and triple agonists in the management of MASH-related fibrosis
papers.summary: Tavaglione and Loomba review the emerging role of GLP-1 mono, dual, and triple agonists in MASH-related fibrosis. These therapies target multiple metabolic and inflammatory pathways and show promising hepatic histological benefits, highlighting their potential to reshape MASH-related fibrosis treatment, while underscoring remaining challenges in treatment duration, tolerability, and individual response.

papers.title: Transforming large language models into medical specialists via knowledge injection
papers.summary: Kim et al. review knowledge-injection strategies transforming general-purpose large language models into medical specialists—internalizing medical knowledge, aligning behavior with clinical norms, and grounding outputs in real-time evidence—plus multimodal integration and agentic AI, charting a roadmap toward safe, trustworthy clinical AI.

papers.title: Surface display of co-stimulatory ligand B7H2 on engineered bacteria enhances tumor immunotherapy
papers.summary: Feng et al. develop surface-engineered bacteria as the living therapeutic for tumor immunotherapy. Bacteria are genetically programmed to display surface-anchored B7H2 to provide co-stimulatory signal of T cells, and a Histag sequence. Coordinating zinc sulfide quantum dots with Histag images tumors and stimulates cGAS/STING pathway.

papers.title: Preferential engagement of the anti-inflammatory ATP/adenosine axis by HIV vaccine candidate with V1-deleted envelope in male rhesus macaques
papers.summary: Silva de Castro, Rahman, Bissa et al. show that an HIV vaccine candidate with an Env V1 deletion reduces SHIV acquisition risk by 81%, whereas an intact-V1 candidate is not efficacious. Protection is linked to mucosal Env IgG, V2-directed ADCC, CD73/ATP-adenosine signaling, and reduced mucosal inflammatory permissiveness to viral infection.

papers.title: Enfortumab vedotin induces immunogenic cell death and shows enhanced preclinical antitumor activity when combined with a PD-1 inhibitor
papers.summary: Olson et al. characterize multiple preclinical mechanisms associated with enfortumab vedotin activity, including direct and bystander cytotoxicity and induction of immunogenic cell death hallmarks. The findings provide mechanistic support for combining enfortumab vedotin with PD-1 inhibitors, such as pembrolizumab, in clinical settings.

papers.title: LungGPT: A unified multimodal system for interpretable diagnosis and clinical decision support of respiratory diseases
papers.summary: Shao et al. present LungGPT, a multimodal artificial intelligence system that fuses clinical features, lab tests and imaging to enhance respiratory healthcare. LungGPT enables accurate diagnoses, early warning of critical illness, and interpretable diagnostic reasoning and decision support, offering a powerful tool to streamline workflows and promote standardization in clinical practice.

papers.title: CRISPRa-identified transcription factors reprogram glioblastoma into dendritic cell-like cells to elicit systemic antitumor immunity
papers.summary: Liu et al. demonstrate a cellular reprogramming strategy that directly transforms glioblastoma cells into functional dendritic cell-like cells. This in situ conversion remodels the tumor microenvironment and elicits robust, systemic antitumor immunity, offering a synergistic and promising approach for clinical cancer immunotherapy.

papers.title: Maternal secretor status and human milk oligosaccharides influence the infant gut resistome
papers.summary: Samarra et al. show that exclusive breastfeeding, through human milk oligosaccharides, shapes the infant gut resistome. Specific human milk oligosaccharides associate with reduced antibiotic resistance genes and modify delivery-related resistome differences, identifying human milk composition as a key regulator of early-life antimicrobial resistance.

papers.title: Fast tumor accumulation and payload release of c-Met targeting aptamer-drug conjugate enables robust anti-tumor efficacy
papers.summary: Liu et al. developed a c-Met-targeting aptamer-drug conjugate (ApDC) that achieved robust anti-tumor efficacy across multiple c-Met-overexpressing tumor models through rapid tumor accumulation and payload release. Its maintained surface receptor expression and favorable pharmacokinetic properties contributed to greater efficacy than a benchmark c-Met-targeting ADC, highlighting its therapeutic promise.

papers.title: Non-genetic remodeling drives leukemia propagation and reveals actionable vulnerabilities in acute myeloid leukemia
papers.summary: Larrue et al. show that serial propagation of AML in xenografts increases leukemia-propagating activity and is accompanied by molecular and drug-response changes. Integrated profiling links these changes to translational and ribosome programs and identifies therapeutic candidates that limit leukemia propagation in vivo.

papers.title: Lysyl oxidase inhibition disrupts mitochondrial homeostasis to create vulnerability to ferroptosis in TNBC
papers.summary: Saatci-Ulukan et al. show that lysyl oxidase (LOX) has non-canonical intracellular functions in promoting glucose metabolism, inhibiting mitophagy, and sustaining redox homeostasis and that inhibiting LOX creates a targetable vulnerability to DHODH-inhibition-mediated ferroptosis in chemo-free setting in triple-negative breast cancer, the deadliest subtype.

papers.title: Development and validation of a serum peptidomic signature for early detection of asymptomatic ovarian cancer: A multi-center prospective study
papers.summary: Asymptomatic ovarian cancer evades detection, driving its high mortality. Li et al. develop ProMS+, a machine-learning model combining seven serum peptidomic markers with age, CA125, and HE4, which achieves high accuracy, outperforming conventional tests. Monte Carlo simulations across diverse risk settings support its potential for high-risk surveillance, pending prospective validation.

papers.title: Pan-tumor spatial transcriptomics reveals conserved properties of tumor organization
papers.summary: Behera et al. characterize spatial biology patterns across 262 solid tumors and 18 tumor types, using spatial transcriptomics and multiplexed immunofluorescence. They find pan-tumor, hierarchically organized “spatial groups” that align with coordinated immunological programs and with outcomes after immune checkpoint blockade therapy in a separate cohort of lung cancer patients.

papers.title: Inhibition of the lipocalin-2-phosphatidylserine axis restores natural killer cell immune surveillance
papers.summary: Qin et al. show that Lipocalin-2 binds phosphatidylserine to promote tumor-associated lipid metabolic reprogramming, impair NK cell immunity, and suppress antitumor surveillance. Pharmacological disruption of the LCN2-PS interaction by semapimod restores innate immune function and inhibits tumor growth.

papers.title: Tumor-on-chip as a personalized platform for rapid drug testing in breast cancer
papers.summary: Helal et al. reports a patient-derived ToC platform that enables rapid (4-day) functional drug profiling of breast cancer samples, including patient biopsies. This platform distinguishes between drug-sensitive and drug-resistant profiles and shows strong concordance with in vivo responses in patient-derived xenograft models, highlighting its potential to guide personalized treatment decisions.

papers.title: Lactobacillus salivarius potentiates gastrointestinal cancer immunotherapy through its metabolite chenodeoxycholic acid
papers.summary: Zhang et al. report Lactobacillus salivarius as a gut commensal enriched in GI cancer patients responsive to anti-PD-1 therapy. L. salivarius potentiates anti-PD-1 efficacy through its metabolite CDCA, which induces tumor immunogenic cell death and M1 macrophage polarization, highlighting the microbiota-metabolite axis as a therapeutic adjuvant for cancer immunotherapy.

papers.title: RET-driven osteoprotegerin expression links medullary thyroid cancer to osteoblastic bone metastases
papers.summary: RET-mutant medullary thyroid cancer (MTC) induces osteoblastic bone metastases by increasing osteoprotegerin and inhibiting osteoclast differentiation. Elevated circulating OPG predicts poor survival, while RET inhibition reduces tumor burden and abnormal bone formation. Guise et al. define a mechanism underlying MTC bone metastasis with biomarker potential.

papers.title: Targeting Regnase-1 in B7-H3-CAR T cells reprograms the tumor microenvironment and enhances antitumor efficacy for osteosarcoma
papers.summary: Adeshakin et al. demonstrated that deletion of Regnase-1 in B7-H3-CAR T cells enhanced their antitumor activity and endowed them with the capability to induce a pro-inflammatory tumor microenvironment. These findings nominate Regnase-1 knockout B7-H3-CAR T cells as a promising cell product for clinical testing in patients with solid tumors.

papers.title: Cell-free DNA genomic and fragmentomic features for early outcome prediction in large B cell lymphoma
papers.summary: Wang et al. develop and validate the ACT score, a tumor-naive WGS-based multimodal cell-free DNA model integrating genomic and fragmentomic features from a single on-treatment plasma sample. ACT identifies large B cell lymphoma patients at high risk of first-line treatment failure and adds prognostic value beyond the International Prognostic Index.

papers.title: Spatiotemporal iron-hijacking hydrogel reprograms host-pathogen iron homeostasis for fungal keratitis therapy
papers.summary: He et al. develop a spatiotemporal iron-hijacking hydrogel (PGaDH) that reprograms host-pathogen iron homeostasis for fungal keratitis therapy. Sequential release of DFP and Ga3+ disrupts fungal iron metabolism while protecting host cells from ferroptosis and inflammation, achieving potent antifungal efficacy and inflammation suppression in both mouse and rabbit models.

papers.title: PARP inhibition enhances the antitumor activity of HER3-DXd in non-small cell lung cancer
papers.summary: Lin et al. show that PARP inhibition enhances the antitumor activity of the HER3-targeting antibody-drug conjugate HER3-DXd in non-small cell lung cancer. The combination induces DNA damage, activates cGAS-STING signaling, and promotes NK cell-mediated antitumor activity across genetically distinct NSCLC models.

papers.title: Cortical-to-pallidal beta cascade underlies network pathophysiology in Parkinson’s disease
papers.summary: Although beta synchrony is a hallmark of Parkinson’s disease, its interactions across motor circuit nodes remain unclear. Choi et al. show that GPe-led high-beta coupling with M1 triggers GPi low-beta amplification and that dopaminergic therapy attenuates this cortical-to-pallidal cascade, revealing a circuit-level mechanism underlying motor dysfunction and its therapeutic modulation.

papers.title: Long-term outcomes of anti-CD19 CAR T cell therapy in refractory myasthenia gravis: A case series
papers.summary: Hegelmaier et al. present 2-year follow-up data from three patients with treatment-refractory myasthenia gravis receiving CAR T cells. All patients show sustained clinical remission. The long-lasting improvement in functional outcomes underscores the impact on daily living and suggests potential clinical benefit of CAR T cell therapy in selected severe neuroimmunological diseases.

papers.title: Faecalibacterium prausnitzii-derived L-arginine ameliorates insomnia by inhibiting POMC-ACTH-cortisol axis
papers.summary: Wang et al. observe F. prausnitzii depletion and reduced L-arginine biosynthesis in subjects with insomnia and show that supplementation with either F. prausnitzii or L-arginine restores sleep duration in mice. They identify the POMC-ACTH-cortisol axis as a key target and propose F. prausnitzii as a potential probiotic for insomnia.

papers.title: CDK8/19 inhibition prevents adaptive resistance to CDK4/6 inhibitors in vitro and in vivo
papers.summary: Non-genetic adaptation curtails CDK4/6 inhibitor therapy. Mack et al. show that adaptive resistance arises through transcriptional reprogramming and is suppressed by inhibition of the Mediator kinases CDK8/19, which enhances CDK4/6 inhibitor efficacy in vitro and in vivo.

papers.title: Scalable generation of hematopoietic stem cell-engineered off-the-shelf mono-specific cytotoxic T cells targeting solid tumors
papers.summary: Zhu et al. develop a scalable, feeder-free platform to generate allogeneic NY-ESO-1-specific T (AlloESO-T) cells from human HSPCs. These mono-specific, cytotoxic T cells combine TCR-driven antigen specificity with NK-like cytotoxicity, achieving enhanced tumor targeting, durable persistence, and reduced CRS/GvHD risk, which support their potential as an off-the-shelf therapy for solid tumors.

papers.title: Humoral pregnancy analyses reveal strategies for fetal protection and aberrancy in miscarriage
papers.summary: Sie et al. performed high-throughput, longitudinal serology during human pregnancy, revealing maternal immunological dynamics. They found enhancement of maternal humoral immunity over pregnancy, both in antibody diversity and in relative concentrations of IgA. Furthermore, they identified spikes in IgA antigen signals preceding miscarriage, targeting both cross-reactive antigens and HLA.

papers.title: Prevention of myopia in a near-primate by supplemental indigo light suggests a hypothesis for the myopia boom
papers.summary: Grytz et al. show that indigo light supplementation prevents lens-induced myopia in tree shrews. The findings suggest that a relative absence of indigo wavelengths in built environments may contribute to the myopia boom and motivate testing indigo-enriched lighting for prevention.

papers.title: Targeting of tripartite neuron-cancer-immune cell crosstalk augments response to chemotherapy and immunotherapy
papers.summary: Jain et al. identify cholinergic nerve-derived acetylcholine as a mediator of immunosuppression in colon cancer and show that localized hydrogel-based delivery of local anesthetics and pharmacological blockade of acetylcholine receptors activate anti-tumor immune responses and enhance the efficacy of chemotherapy and immunotherapy.

papers.title: The evolution of iPSC-based cell therapy across autologous and allogeneic pathways
papers.summary: Wang et al. review the evolution of iPSC-based cell therapy, from early proof-of-concept studies to clinical translation and regulatory approval, showing how advances in reprogramming, manufacturing, and immune engineering have shaped autologous and allogeneic iPSC therapies into complementary clinical platforms.

papers.title: This week in charts: RA’s insatiable appetite, Novartis’ big slide and a reverse merger spree
papers.summary: RA Capital has already participated in four biotech financings in September. Meanwhile, Janus Henderson has been the year's most prolific backer of biotech reverse merger deals, according to Gilmartin Group.

papers.title: Karyopharm pushes off debt payment; Amgen eyes broader Imdelltra use
papers.summary: Karyopharm bought an extra month to negotiate with creditors or pursue a deal. Elsewhere, BridgeBio Pharma’s oncology spinout shook up its development plans and a brain-focused gene therapy startup banked $275 million.

papers.title: mRNA cancer vaccines’ biggest barriers to market
papers.summary: Manufacturing hurdles are just one challenge the industry must overcome to commercialize personalized mRNA cancer vaccines.

papers.title: FDA places partial hold on Biohaven’s epilepsy drug
papers.summary: Announced mere weeks after Biohaven sold off rights to the therapy, opakalim, the halt affects a study some analysts believe is necessary to support a potential approval.

papers.title: Andy Plump, architect of Takeda’s R&D overhaul, to retire next year
papers.summary: Plump joined Takeda during a turbulent period, pushed the company to work more closely with young biotechs and will leave it with what CEO Julie Kim called a “lasting foundation.”

papers.title: A booming business on Wall Street would love more biotechs to quietly die
papers.summary: Once disparaged, reverse mergers have become so popular that some deal experts question whether there are enough quality shell companies to meet the demand.

papers.title: Tyra disappoints investors with bladder cancer data
papers.summary: Remission rates observed in a Phase 2 trial fell short of Wall Street's expectations, though some analysts believe the company should see better results in late-stage testing.

papers.title: Kura spins diabetes work into a Lilly-backed biotech startup
papers.summary: Caspian Therapeutics aims to develop menin inhibitors, which have proven effective against leukemia, for diabetes and other cardiometabolic conditions.

papers.title: FDA gains ‘continuity’ as Mikhail, Davis named permanent CBER, CDER leaders
papers.summary: After almost two years of turnover in the FDA’s top ranks, the new appointments should help ease concerns about more turmoil ahead, one analyst said.

papers.title: A new immuno-oncology play raises $225M for a next-generation drug
papers.summary: Solstice Oncology is advancing a medicine from China’s Harbour BioMed that it believes is able to address the weaknesses of drugs aimed at CTLA-4, a popular but tricky cancer immunotherapy target.

GSK’s risvutatug rezetecan has achieved a median overall survival of 18.5 months in a phase 3 trial, painting the antibody-drug conjugate as a threat to Amgen and Merck & Co. in the lung cancer field.
The FDA has delayed its approval decision for Exelixis’ oral kinase inhibitor in combination with Roche’s Tecentriq for the treatment of metastatic colorectal cancer.

Revolution Medicines recently made history with the approval of its RAS inhibitor Rasonque for advanced pancreatic cancer. But behind RevMed is an entire field of biotechs working to broaden the reach of RAS-targeting drugs.

The announcement from Merck & Co. and Moderna last month that their mRNA cancer vaccine had successfully lengthened patient survival in a phase 3 study affirmed the two companies' years of hard work and reignited hopes for the field of personalized medicine.
Officials rubbed shoulders with business leaders in a 19th-floor meeting room to celebrate the launch of Singapore’s newest Overseas Centre.
Takeda President of Research and Development Andy Plump, M.D., Ph.D., is leaving the company in June after twelve years in the position.

Following the removal of five scientists from its annual conference in June, members of the American Diabetes Association have launched a boycott of the organization that includes halting the review of grants and new articles submitted to the ADA’s flagship journal, Diabetes Care.

In his first interview after taking the reins of the FDA’s Oncology Center of Excellence, Angelo de Claro, M.D., is outlining a regulatory agenda that prioritizes organizational strength and continued regulatory modernization.
Novartis’ recent dual clinical setbacks have prompted questions from a major shareholder about the board’s oversight of dealmaking.

It may have seemed like an ordinary Wednesday afternoon at MassBio’s headquarters in Technology Square, but the black SUV parked outside was a telltale sign that the Cambridge, Massachusetts-based biotech trade group was playing host to a government official.

The FDA has put enrollment in trials of Biohaven’s epilepsy drug candidate BHV-7000 on hold in response to findings from rodent tests, dealing a blow to an asset covered by a pending $350 million deal.
Frazier Life Sciences (FLS) has stacked up another sizable biotech-focused capital commitment, netting more than $1.1 billion for its long-running public fund.
Andy Plump, M.D., Ph.D., president of research and development at Takeda, is set to leave the company in June.
Clinical research company nPhase has launched an end-to-end clinical data management platform designed to help trial sponsors leverage trial results with AI.
Kura Oncology has spun out a biotech armed with $50 million in fresh funding to take forward a next-generation diabetes treatment.
Luma Group announced the final close of its inaugural life sciences venture capital fund totaling $410 million.
Neuro-focused Encoded Therapeutics has bagged a $275 million series F round to support its Dravet syndrome asset and scale up its internal manufacturing capabilities.

Tyra Biosciences has reported initial phase 2 data on dabogratinib in bladder cancer, putting the biotech on course to start a registrational study next year. But the biotech’s stock fell in premarket trading after the complete response rate fell short of the level targeted by analysts.
Medtech and testing giant Labcorp has bought out MLM Medical Labs to help grow its geographic footprint for laboratory services.

In a stabilizing move, the Department of Health and Human Services announced Tuesday afternoon that it has tapped Michael Davis, M.D., Ph.D., and Karim Mikhail—who’ve been serving as acting directors of CDER and CBER, respectively—to occupy their posts on a permanent basis.
The Fierce Biotech Fundraising Tracker records venture capital rounds of $50 million or more secured by biotechs.
As always, if you know of layoffs occurring at a biotech, please reach out to the Fierce Biotech editorial team.
Abbot received FDA clearance for its latest-generation catheter that allows physicians more flexibility when treating atrial fibrillation in patients.
Solstice Oncology has secured $225 million in series A funding to advance a next-gen immunotherapy that the biotech hopes will turn “darkness to light” for cancer care.
Schrödinger announced the launch of new immune disease-focused Tectora Therapeutics, which comes online with a $55 million series A financing round.

papers.summary: Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 07 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-026-01293-x Kumaran et al. show that large language models making decisions on when to answer a question or abstain from answering can be influenced by boosting or suppressing confidence signals in the model.

papers.summary: Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 03 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-026-01289-7 Wang et al. introduce a hardware-efficient quantum neural operator that overcomes classical linear capacity limits. Using an implicit quadratic frame, it offers accelerated expressivity for solving differential equations in the noisy intermediate-scale quantum era.

papers.summary: Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 03 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-026-01295-9 RNA structure and function are hard to infer because annotations are scarce, despite abundant sequence data. papers.title: Steering machine reasoning with brain signals

papers.title: Implicit-bias-like patterns in reasoning models
papers.summary: Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 01 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-026-01300-1 Lee and Lai study bias-like processing differences in large language reasoning models and find that, for most models, processing stereotypical information takes less computational effort than processing counter-stereotypical information.

papers.title: Enhancing reproducibility in hybrid Earth system models
papers.summary: Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 28 August 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-026-01299-5 AI integration in Earth system models enhances prediction and modelling capabilities but also amplifies challenges for reproducibility. This Perspective introduces a framework for assessing reproducibility and provides practical ways to strengthen reproducibility in hybrid Earth system models.

papers.title: Large language models as uncertainty-calibrated optimizers for experimental discovery
papers.summary: Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 28 August 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-026-01283-z Although language models can be helpful in molecular design, they are not typically calibrated for uncertainty. Rankovic and colleagues present a method to train language models while taking into account the uncertainty of the data.
